name: systemctl

examples.does: Running or not, since when, and its last log lines
Stop and start a service
Units that failed
Start now and at every boot
Will it start at boot
Scheduled timers: next and last run
The unit file and any overrides, as systemd reads them
Add an override (kept when the package updates)
Re-read unit files after editing them by hand

pitfalls: After editing a unit file by hand, run daemon-reload, or systemd keeps using the old one.
reload re-reads config without stopping; not every service supports it. restart always works but drops connections.

name: journalctl

examples.does: The last 50 log lines of one service
Follow a service's log live (Ctrl-C stops)
Errors and worse since this boot
Everything from the last hour
Kernel messages from the previous boot (after a crash)
How much disk the journal uses
Delete the oldest archived logs until the journal is under 500 MB

pitfalls: Without sudo, or membership of the adm or systemd-journal group, you may only see your own logs.
The previous boot's logs exist only if the journal is stored on disk (/var/log/journal).

name: systemd-analyze
summary: Boot time and unit file checks
tasks: check a unit file for mistakes

examples.does: Units sorted by how long they took to start
The chain of units that set the boot time
Check a unit file for mistakes
How much a service is sandboxed, with a score

name: timedatectl
summary: Time, time zone and time sync

examples.does: Local time, UTC, time zone, and whether the clock is synced
Valid time zone names
Set the time zone
Time server, offset and poll interval (systemd-timesyncd)

pitfalls: In an air-gapped network, time sync needs an internal NTP server set in /etc/systemd/timesyncd.conf.

name: hostnamectl
summary: Show or set the host name

examples.does: Host name, OS, kernel and hardware
Set the host name

pitfalls: Also update the name in /etc/hosts, or sudo may print 'unable to resolve host'.

name: crontab

examples.does: Your scheduled jobs
Edit your scheduled jobs
Another user's jobs

pitfalls: System-wide jobs are also in /etc/crontab and /etc/cron.d/, and many are systemd timers (systemctl list-timers).
Cron runs with a minimal PATH. Use full paths in jobs.

examples.does: Dry run: shows what would happen, changes nothing
Rotate now, even if it is not due

name: dmesg

examples.does: The last 50 kernel messages with readable times
Only errors and warnings
Follow new kernel messages (Ctrl-C stops)

pitfalls: The -T times can drift after suspend. journalctl -k has exact times.
